newsitem.title: UK: London bourse sets plans for order-driven market.
newsitem.headline: London bourse sets plans for order-driven market.

text.p: The London Stock Exchange (LSE) on Thursday took another step towards the introduction of automated order-driven trading for FTSE 100 stocks with the publication of the operational and regulatory framework for the new system.
The electronic order book system is unlikely to be implemented in spring 1997, as originally hoped, but looks likely to begin sometime in autumn 1997.

For FTSE 100 stocks, the LSE will replace the current market-making system with an order book, the LSE said. Investors will place orders through market firms and once on the order book, orders will be executed automatically.

The regulatory structure will allow the negotiation of large trades away from the order book. Firms will therefore be able to continue to commit capital to large trades, thus providing liquidity to the London market, the exchange said.

"As a result of extensive consultation over the last nine months, the trading environment which we plan to deliver will combine the most important features of the current system with the increased flexibility and liquidity that a successful order book will bring," LSE chief executive Gavin Casey said in a statement.

Publishing the full service definition for the electronic order book, the LSE said it would consult with the market on the appropriate structure for non-FTSE 100 stocks, which meantime would continue to be traded as at present. of the Exchange's earlier proposals, has been dropped as it is no longer required following the decision by Chancellor Kenneth Clarke to extend stamp duty relief to all Exchange intermediaries.
